summary: Describes a way for OSPF routers to gracefully handle unexpected overflow of their link-state database. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary:
Every OSPF router in an area has to hold the same map of the network. In a big network that map can grow too large for some routers to hold.

This RFC says what a router should do when that happens: stop accepting new external routes, withdraw the ones it published itself, and carry on with what it has. All the routers then end up with the same smaller map.

subtitle: How an OSPF router keeps a link-state database from growing past what it can hold.

tldr.problem: OSPF requires every router in an area to hold an identical copy of the link-state database, and in a large network that database can grow larger than a router's memory.
tldr.mechanism: Every router is given a limit on the number of external route advertisements it will hold. When a router reaches that limit it drops what it has received, flushes the external routes it published itself, and stops publishing any more until the database shrinks.
tldr.outcome: All the routers converge on the same smaller database, so routing inside the network stays correct while the overflow lasts. The document is Experimental and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Default ospfExitOverflowInterval
facts.value: 0, meaning the router stays in OverflowState until it is restarted

sections.title: The Problem and the Overflow Mechanism
sections.content:
OSPF requires that all OSPF routers within a single area maintain an identical copy of the OSPF link-state database. However, when the size of the link-state database becomes very large, some routers may be unable to keep the entire database due to resource shortages, and this is called database overflow. A regional network, for example, may have a very large OSPF database because it is importing a large number of external routes into OSPF. Unless database overflow is handled correctly, routers end up with inconsistent views of the network, possibly leading to incorrect routing.

One way of handling database overflow is to encase routers having limited resources within OSPF stub areas or NSSAs. AS-external-LSAs are omitted from these areas' link-state databases, thereby controlling database size. However, unexpected database overflows cannot be handled in that manner, and this memo describes a way of dynamically limiting database size under overflow conditions.

The basic mechanism has five steps. A parameter, ospfExtLsdbLimit, is configured in each router indicating the maximum number of AS-external-LSAs, excluding those describing the default route, that are allowed in the link-state database; this parameter must be the same in all routers in the routing domain, and synchronization is achieved via network management. In any router's database, the number of AS-external-LSAs, excluding default, is never allowed to exceed ospfExtLsdbLimit: if a router receives a non-default AS-external-LSA that would cause the limit to be exceeded, it drops the LSA and does not acknowledge it. If the number of non-default AS-external-LSAs in a router's database hits ospfExtLsdbLimit, the router flushes all the non-default AS-external-LSAs that it has itself originated and goes into OverflowState. While in OverflowState the router refuses to originate any non-default AS-external-LSAs. Optionally, the router can attempt to leave OverflowState after the configurable parameter ospfExitOverflowInterval has elapsed since entering OverflowState, and only at that point can it resume originating non-default AS-external-LSAs.

The reason for limiting non-default AS-external-LSAs but not other LSA types is twofold. The non-default AS-external LSAs are the most likely to dominate database size in networks with huge databases, and they can be viewed as optional in the sense that the router can probably be monitored or reconfigured without them.

The method has four desirable properties. After a short period of convergence, all routers have identical link-state databases, containing fewer than ospfExtLsdbLimit non-default AS-external-LSAs. Routing within the OSPF Autonomous System remains intact at all times, so the routers stay manageable. Default routing to external destinations also remains intact, which hopefully means a large amount of external connectivity is preserved, although possibly taking less efficient routes. And if ospfExitOverflowInterval is configured, the OSPF system recovers fully and automatically, without network management intervention, from transient database overflow conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is simple: every router holds at most a set number of external routes. When one reaches that number it withdraws its own external routes and stops publishing more, so that every router ends up with the same smaller set.

sections.title: The Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
Two configuration parameters are added to support the database overflow functionality, and they are set by network management.

ospfExtLsdbLimit gives the number of non-default AS-external-LSAs at which a router enters OverflowState. The router never holds more than ospfExtLsdbLimit non-default AS-external-LSAs in its database. The value MUST be set identically in all routers attached to the OSPF backbone and in any regular OSPF area. The memo does not pertain to routers inside OSPF stub areas or NSSAs, since such routers do not receive AS-external-LSAs. If the limit is not set identically in all routers, then when the database overflows the routers will not converge on a common link-state database, incorrect routing, possibly including routing loops, will result, and constant retransmission of AS-external-LSAs will occur. Identical setting is achieved and ensured by network management. When the limit is set, the router must have some way to guarantee that it can hold that many non-default AS-external-LSAs in its link-state database; one way of doing this is to preallocate resources such as memory for the configured number of LSAs.

ospfExitOverflowInterval is the number of seconds that, after entering OverflowState, a router will attempt to leave OverflowState, which allows it to originate non-default AS-external-LSAs again. When set to 0 the router will not leave OverflowState until it is restarted, and the default setting is 0. It is not necessary for this parameter to be configured the same in all routers: a smaller value may be set in those routers that originate the more important AS-external-LSAs. In fact, setting it the same may cause problems, as multiple routers would attempt to leave OverflowState simultaneously, so the value must be jittered by randomly varying it within plus or minus 10 percent before use.
sections.plainLanguage: Two numbers control the behaviour: how many external routes a router will hold, and how long it stays in the restricted state before trying again. The first has to be the same everywhere; the second is deliberately made slightly different on each router so they do not all recover at once.

sections.title: Entering, Operating In and Leaving OverflowState
sections.content:
A router enters OverflowState when the number of non-default AS-external-LSAs in the database hits ospfExtLsdbLimit. There are two cases when this can occur: when receiving an LSA during flooding, where an LSA which does not already have a database instance is added, and when the router originates a non-default AS-external-LSA itself. Whenever the router enters OverflowState it flushes all the non-default AS-external-LSAs that it itself had originated, through the premature aging scheme described in the OSPF specification. Only self-originated LSAs are flushed; those originated by other routers are kept in the link-state database.

While in OverflowState, flooding is modified. If a non-default AS-external-LSA has been received that has no current database instance and would cause the count of non-default AS-external-LSAs to exceed ospfExtLsdbLimit, then that LSA is discarded: it is not installed in the link-state database, nor is it acknowledged. When all routers have identical values for ospfExtLsdbLimit, as required, this modification is only invoked during a short period of convergence. During convergence there will be retransmissions of LSAs, but after convergence the retransmissions cease, as the routers settle on a database having fewer than ospfExtLsdbLimit non-default AS-external-LSAs.

Non-default AS-external-LSAs are still accepted in OverflowState in three situations: if the LSA updates an LSA that currently exists in the router's link-state database; if the LSA has an LS age of MaxAge, which is always accepted and processed by the normal procedures; and if adding the LSA to the database would keep the number of non-default AS-external-LSAs less than or equal to ospfExtLsdbLimit.

While in OverflowState a router does not originate non-default AS-external-LSAs, so the only AS-external-LSAs it originates have Link State ID 0.0.0.0, which is the default route. If a router in OverflowState receives a self-originated non-default AS-external-LSA, it responds by flushing it from the routing domain using the premature aging scheme.

If ospfExitOverflowInterval is non-zero, then as soon as a router enters OverflowState it sets a timer equal to the value of ospfExitOverflowInterval, plus or minus a random value in the range of 10 percent. When this timer fires, the router leaves OverflowState and begins originating non-default AS-external-LSAs again. This allows a router to recover automatically from transient overflow conditions. For example, an AS boundary router that imports a great many AS-external-LSAs may crash; other routers may then start importing the routes, but until the crashed router is restarted or its LSAs age out there will be a much larger database than usual. Since such an overflow is guaranteed to go away in MaxAge seconds, which is one hour, automatic recovery may be appropriate if the overflow happens off-hours. As soon as the router leaves OverflowState it is again eligible to re-enter it.
sections.plainLanguage: On entering the restricted state the router withdraws only the external routes it published itself, and it drops new external routes rather than acknowledging them. When the timer fires it starts publishing again, unless the database is still too full.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
Suppose a router implements the database overflow logic, with an ospfExtLsdbLimit of 10,000 and an ospfExitOverflowInterval of 600 seconds. Suppose further that the router itself is originating 400 non-default AS-external-LSAs, and that the current number of non-default AS-external-LSAs in its database is 9,997.

It receives a Link State Update packet from a neighbour containing 6 non-default AS-external-LSAs, none of which have current database copies. The first two LSAs are installed in the database. The third LSA is also installed, but causes the router to go into OverflowState. Going into OverflowState causes the router to flush, through premature aging, its 400 self-originated non-default LSAs. Those 400 LSAs are still considered to be part of the link-state database until their re-flooding, with age set to MaxAge, is acknowledged, so for that reason the last three LSAs in the received update are discarded without being acknowledged.

After some small period of time all routers converge on a common database, having fewer than 10,000 non-default AS-external-LSAs. During this convergence period there may be some link-state retransmissions: for example, the sender of the Link State Update packet may retransmit the three LSAs that were discarded. If this retransmission happens after the flushing of the 400 self-originated LSAs is acknowledged, the three LSAs will then be accepted.

Going into OverflowState also causes the router to set a timer that will fire some time between 540 and 660 seconds later. When this timer fires, the router leaves OverflowState and re-originates its 400 non-default AS-external-LSAs, provided the current database has fewer than 9600, which is 10,000 minus 400, non-default AS-external-LSAs. If there are more than 9600, the timer is simply restarted.
sections.plainLanguage: The example follows one router as it fills up, throws away its own routes, waits, and then puts them back once there is room again.

sections.title: The Network Manager's Response
sections.content:
Once the link-state database has overflowed, it may take intervention by network management before all routing is restored, although if the overflow condition is transient routing may be restored automatically. An overflow condition is indicated by SNMP traps. Possible responses by a network manager include increasing the value of ospfExtLsdbLimit, perhaps because it had been set too conservatively and the routers are able to support larger databases than they are currently configured for; isolating routers having limited resources within OSPF stub areas or NSSAs, which would allow the value of ospfExtLsdbLimit to be increased in the remaining routers; and re-evaluating the need to import certain external routes, so that if the limit cannot be increased the more important routes continue to be imported, by turning off the importing of less important routes.

Four related OSPF MIB variables have been defined to support the procedure. ospfExtLsdbLimit is the maximum number of non-default AS-external-LSAs that can be stored within the database, and if set to -1 there is no limit. ospfExitOverflowInterval is the number of seconds that, after entering OverflowState, a router will attempt to leave it, and when set to 0 the router will not leave until it is restarted. ospfLsdbOverflow is a trap indicating that the number of non-default AS-external-LSAs has exceeded or equalled ospfExtLsdbLimit, in other words that the router is entering OverflowState. ospfLsdbApproachingOverflow is a trap indicating that the number of non-default AS-external-LSAs has exceeded ninety percent of ospfExtLsdbLimit.
sections.plainLanguage: The manager is told about the overflow by a trap, and has three levers: raise the limit, put the smallest routers behind a stub area, or stop importing the least important external routes.

sections.title: Operational Experience, Enhancements and Security
sections.content:
The scheme has been implemented in the Proteon router for a number of years, with two differences. The router did not leave OverflowState until it was restarted, so ospfExitOverflowInterval was always 0. And default AS-external-LSAs were not separated from non-default AS-external-LSAs. Operationally the scheme performed as expected: during overflow conditions, the routers converged on a common database having fewer than a configured number of AS-external-LSAs.

Possible enhancements to the overflow scheme include limiting other LSA types in a similar fashion, with the exception of the transit LSAs, the router-LSAs and network-LSAs; one could limit the number of summary-LSAs or group-membership-LSAs. And rather than flushing all of its non-default AS-external-LSAs when entering OverflowState, a router could flush a fixed number each time the database size hits the limit, which would let it prioritise its external LSAs and flush the least important ones first.

The Security Considerations section of RFC 1765 says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism had been running in a router for years before the RFC was written, and worked as described. The RFC also suggests ways to extend it to other kinds of route.

viz.caption: The five steps of the overflow mechanism (RFC 1765, Section 1)

items.title: Set a limit
items.text: ospfExtLsdbLimit is configured on every router, giving the maximum number of non-default AS-external LSAs the database may hold.

items.title: Never exceed the limit
items.text: A received non-default AS-external-LSA that would push the count over the limit is dropped and not acknowledged.

items.title: Enter OverflowState
items.text: When the count reaches the limit, the router flushes its own non-default AS-external LSAs and enters OverflowState.

items.title: Stop originating
items.text: While in OverflowState the router refuses to originate any non-default AS-external LSA.

items.title: Recover
items.text: If ospfExitOverflowInterval is set, the router tries to leave OverflowState after that many seconds and can then originate again.

viz.caption: The parameters and traps used by the scheme (RFC 1765, Section 2.1 and Appendix A)

cells: Maximum number of non-default AS-external LSAs in the link-state database. Must be identical in every router on the backbone and in any regular area. A value of -1 means no limit.
Seconds a router waits before trying to leave OverflowState. The value is jittered by plus or minus 10 percent, and 0 means the router stays in OverflowState until it is restarted.
A trap signalling that the number of non-default AS-external LSAs has reached or exceeded the limit.
A trap signalling that the number has exceeded ninety percent of the limit.
